title: The Typo That Took Down the Internet

post.author: u/calderline_nights_hafsa
post.title: I'm the night control engineer at a power company. At 02:15 our outage map showed every home in the region dark. The lights in my control room never flickered.

blocks.text: I'm Hafsa, the night control engineer at Calderline Power. We carry electricity to 180,000 homes across the Ostermere region. From the control room I watch the outage map: a screen with a dot for every home, lit while it has power.

Every home has a smart meter, an electricity meter that sends its reading over the phone network every minute. If a meter has not answered for 15 minutes, the map shows that home dark. That is how we find a fault at night, before anyone phones.

The readings come in through 50 servers, computers that answer other machines, named mr-01 to mr-50. Each carries about 3,600 meters and can take 6,000 at most. If a server stops, its meters move to another one within a minute. So we need at least 30 servers up. That 30 is our minimum.
Updates go in by restart, in three steps. A server stops. It checks the readings it has stored. Then it starts again. That takes 20 minutes, and meanwhile its meters answer through the other servers.

Each week three servers are restarted with our restart tool. You type it into a terminal, a text window for typed instructions. Before tonight, every restart listed the names one by one: restart mr-01 mr-02 mr-03. Their meters moved, and nobody ever saw a dark dot.
The tool also takes a name pattern: a short way to write many names at once.
This week's restart fell to Ksawery, our junior engineer, on call for the first time: at home, but ready to work. He tried a pattern instead of listing names.

The first line below is what he typed at 02:00. A * means any characters, so mr-* means every name starting mr-. He meant mr-0[1-3], where [1-3] means one character, 1, 2 or 3: only mr-01, mr-02 and mr-03. The other lines are the tool's reply.

restart mr-*
restarting mr-01 mr-02 mr-03 ... mr-50
done
The tool asked nothing and showed no count. It knew no minimum, so all 50 servers stopped together. 180,000 meters looked for another server and found none.
At 02:15 the map went dark. Every dot. The whole region.
The lights in the control room, fed from the same lines, never flickered.

The dispatcher had three crews pulling on boots. I checked the line readings: power was flowing on every line. I held the crews. At 02:20 the servers finished their restart, the meters answered, and the map lit up again, every dot at once.

blocks.label: outage_map_0200_0225.png

diagram.aria: 02:00 to 02:25. At 02:00 the restart tool stops all 50 meter servers; they are restarting until 02:20 and up after that. All 180,000 meters are silent from 02:00 to 02:20, with no server to move to. The outage map shows every home with power until 02:15, then 180,000 homes dark from 02:15 to 02:20, then every home with power again.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from the tool's log and the map's history. At 02:00 restart mr-* stopped all 50 servers, so 180,000 meters had nowhere to move. Fifteen minutes of silence later, at 02:15, the map drew every home dark. At 02:20 the servers were back and every meter answered.

blocks.text: Ksawery has offered to come off the rota. Our manager says restarts happen in daylight from now on. The tool did exactly what it was told. It had no guard rail: no check of its own that could have stopped it. What should we change before next week's restart?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: Look at the screens before you look at the people. What did the tool show Ksawery before it acted? The number he meant was 3; where could he have seen the number it was about to take? Then your 30. You wrote it in your post. Where else is it written, and who reads it at 02:00? Some tools offer a dry run, a rehearsal that prints what a command would do without doing it. Last, for every fix you're offered: next week, if someone types a pattern wrong, which part of your system notices before the meters do?

replies.author: u/calderline_nights_hafsa
replies.text: Before it acted, nothing. After, fifty names and 'done'. The 30 lives in our shift handbook. Our tool has no dry run.

comments.author: u/read_the_glob_tsegaye
comments.text: Respectfully, this is a people problem. Nobody should be on call who can't read a glob, which is what admins call a name pattern like mr-*. The tool did exactly what it was told; tools always will. Retrain him on patterns, give him a test, and keep him off restarts until he passes. Change the tool for one bad night and you slow down everyone who types it right.

comments.author: u/four_eyes_wairimu
comments.text: Where I work, nothing that can stop a whole service runs on one person's say-so. The engineer posts the command, a second engineer reads it and approves it, and only then will the tool run. Two people rarely make the same slip in the same minute, and it costs five minutes.

reply.prompt: Next week's restart is on Tuesday night. What should Calderline change before then? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Retrain Ksawery on name patterns, and keep him off restarts until he passes a test.
options.verdict: One person fixed, the tool unchanged
options.part2: Ksawery spent two weeks on patterns and passed. On Tuesday he typed restart mr-0[1-3]: in the sim, 3 of 50 matched, 10,800 meters moved within a minute, and nothing went dark. The tool was unchanged. In March a senior engineer in a hurry meant mr-1[0-2] and typed mr-[1-3]*. In the sim: 30 of 50 servers stopped at once, the 20 left could carry only 120,000 meters, and at 02:15 the map showed 60,000 homes dark. He had passed every test there is. Tsegaye's rule took one person away from the tool; it left the slip in the tool for everyone else.
options.senior: Training helps, and blaming a person for a slip that any tired expert can make teaches everyone to hide slips. The tool still takes whatever matches, all at once, with no floor, so the next wrong pattern, typed by anyone, stops as many servers as it names. A blameless post-mortem asks what let one typed line take the whole region, and the answer is the tool, not the typist. Fix the system so the same slip does little harm, then train people as well.

options.text: Have a second engineer approve every restart pattern before the tool is allowed to run.
options.verdict: Two readers, the same blind spot
options.part2: From Tuesday a second engineer approved every restart. In the sim I turned the approver on and replayed tonight. At 02:00 the log reads: Second engineer reads "restart mr-*" and approves. He saw the same line Ksawery saw, the pattern and never the count, and mr-* reads like 'the meter servers'. At 02:15 the map showed 180,000 homes dark, as before. The approvals did catch two slips that spring, a wrong server number and a missing letter, and they left a record of who changed what. They could not catch this one, because nothing on either screen said 50.
options.senior: A second pair of eyes catches what can be seen: a wrong name, an obvious typo. A pattern hides its own size; mr-* and mr-0[1-3] look alike, and the reviewer reads text, not the list it expands to. Reviews are worth keeping as a record and for unusual changes, but on routine commands people approve quickly, and two people share the same blind spot. Put the check where the facts are: in the tool, which knows the count and the floor.

options.text: Allow restarts only in the daytime, when senior engineers are at their desks too.
options.part2: Our manager moved restarts to noon. In the sim, the same mr-* at 12:00: 50 of 50 matched, and at 12:15 the map showed 180,000 homes dark, in full daylight. This time customers' phones rang too, and the crews got as far as the yard. The senior engineers were at their desks and watched the map go dark with everyone else: the tool still stopped all 50 at once, and each server still needed its 20 minutes. Daytime also meant the restart now touched the busiest hours.
options.senior: Moving a dangerous command to a different hour changes who is watching, not what the command does. The same pattern stops the same servers at noon, and more people are hurt or alarmed by it. Daytime changes can be sensible for risky one-off work, so experts are near, but they are no guard rail: nothing in the tool counts, refuses or slows down. Make the command itself safe, and then it can run at whatever hour hurts least.

options.text: Make the tool refuse to go below a minimum, and restart a few servers at a time.
options.part2: Ksawery and I added two rules to the tool: never leave fewer than 30 servers up, and restart 3 at a time, waiting for each three to come back. In the sim, the same mr-* at 02:00 printed: 50 of 50 match. Minimum 30 up. 3 at a time. Restarting 3 now (mr-01 to mr-03), holding 47. 10,800 meters moved within a minute, the next three went at 02:20, and the map never showed a dark home. With the minimum alone, 20 went at once and the other 30 carried exactly 6,000 each: safe, with no room to spare, so we kept both. On Tuesday Ksawery typed his pattern, read '3 of 50 match', and nobody saw a thing.
options.senior: Guard rails belong in the tool, because the tool knows what a person can't see at 02:00. A minimum is a floor the tool refuses to go below, so no input, however wrong, removes what the service needs. Acting a few at a time makes a mistake small and slow enough to notice. Add the count before acting and a dry run, so people see the size of what they asked for. AWS made the same changes after its 2017 S3 outage. Keep the floor worked out from the real load, with a margin, and check it whenever the load grows.

sim.title: Replay the restart, with and without guard rails
sim.lede: You're Hafsa at 01:55, five minutes before the weekly restart. 50 servers, mr-01 to mr-50, carry 180,000 smart meters, 3,600 each; a server takes at most 6,000. A restart stops a server for 20 minutes. Its meters move to servers with room a minute later, or stay silent if there is none, and the outage map shows a home dark after 15 minutes of silence. Pick the pattern typed at 02:00 and the restart tool's guard rails: show the count first (Ksawery meant 3, so he stops if it says otherwise), a minimum of servers kept up, how many it restarts at a time, a dry run, a second engineer who approves, and the hour it runs. Then run the night a minute at a time, to the 15-minute mark, or to the end.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to the 15-minute mark as now. mr-* matched 50 of 50 and the map shows 180,000 homes dark at 02:15; at 02:20 they come back. Switch to mr-0[1-3]: 3 of 50, 10,800 meters move at 02:01, nothing dark. Try mr-[1-3]*: 30 of 50, 60,000 dark. Turn on the second approver: he approves restart mr-*, 180,000 dark. Run it at 12:00: 180,000 dark at 12:15. Now set a minimum of 30 and 3 at a time: mr-01 to mr-03 at 02:00, the next three at 02:20, nothing dark. Then try a dry run, and showing the count.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke. The restart tool did what it was built to do: it restarted every server the pattern matched, all at once. mr-* matched 50 of 50, no meter had a server to move to, and after 15 minutes of silence the map drew 180,000 homes dark while the power flowed. Make the tool refuse to go below the 30 servers the meters need, and restart a few at a time.

steps.title: A pattern is a question the tool answers for you.
steps.text: The tool handles a pattern in steps. First it reads the pattern. Then it compares it with each of the 50 server names. Then it keeps every name that fits, and acts on all of them. A * fits any characters, so mr-* fits every name that starts mr-. [1-3] fits one character, 1, 2 or 3, so mr-0[1-3] fits three names. The person typing sees the pattern; only the tool sees the list it turns into. Tonight's tool printed the list after acting, never before, and never as a number.

steps.title: The map counts silence, not darkness.
steps.text: A reading's path goes in steps: the meter sends it each minute, a server takes it, the map marks the home as answering. When a server stops, its meters try another server; if one has room, they are back within a minute. If none has room, they stay silent. After 15 minutes of silence the map draws the home dark, because on a normal night that is what silence means. Every restart before tonight stopped three servers, the other 47 had room, and no meter was silent past a minute. Tonight no server was left, so every meter was silent for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Where the minimum comes from.
steps.text: Work it out in steps. 180,000 meters, at most 6,000 on each server: 180,000 divided by 6,000 is 30 servers, the least that can carry every meter. With 20 up they carry 120,000, which is why mr-[1-3]*, matching 30 servers, leaves 60,000 homes dark. At exactly 30 up every server is full, with no room for one meter more, so a sensible floor adds a margin. And the number moves: more meters means a higher floor, so the tool should work it out from today's load, not from a number written once.

steps.title: Guard rails: show it, refuse it, slow it down.
steps.text: Each guard rail catches something different. Showing the count before acting, '50 of 50 servers match', turns an invisible list into a number a person can compare with what they meant. A dry run prints the whole plan and changes nothing. A minimum makes the tool refuse to go below what the service needs, whatever was typed. Restarting a few at a time makes any mistake small and slow: 3 servers at once costs a minute of silence, and there is time to notice before the next three. The first two depend on someone reading; the last two work even when nobody does.

steps.title: Why a second person misses it.
steps.text: A two-person check works in steps: one writes the command, another reads it and approves, then it runs. The approver reads the same line, restart mr-*, with the same blind spot, because nothing on the screen shows the 50. Approval of routine commands also becomes quick and automatic. Keep reviews for unusual changes and for the record, but put the safety where the facts are: the tool knows the count, the load and the floor, and a reviewer does not.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for Tuesday. The engineer types restart and a pattern into the restart tool. The tool shows how many servers match, 50 of 50 for mr-*, keeps at least 30 servers up, and restarts 3 at a time. The 50 meter servers then have 47 up and 3 restarting. The 180,000 smart meters send readings to the servers, and the servers tell the outage map who is answering: 0 homes dark.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for Tuesday. The restart tool shows how many servers a pattern matches, refuses to leave fewer than 30 up, and restarts 3 at a time. In the sim the same mr-* restarts mr-01 to mr-03 at 02:00 and the next three at 02:20; their meters move within a minute, and the map never shows a dark home.

fix.title: The fix: a floor in the tool, and a few at a time
fix.text: Give the restart tool two rules. First, a minimum: it refuses any restart that would leave fewer than 30 servers up, the least that can carry 180,000 meters at 6,000 each, and better a few more for margin. Second, a batch size: it restarts 3 at a time and waits for them to come back before the next three. Then add the two that help people see: print the count before acting, '50 of 50 servers match', and ask for that number back; and offer a dry run that prints the plan and changes nothing. Check it in the sim: with a minimum of 30 and 3 at a time, mr-* restarts mr-01 to mr-03 at 02:00 and mr-04 to mr-06 at 02:20, and the map never shows a dark home.

limits: A minimum is only as good as its number. 30 is right for 180,000 meters at 6,000 each; when meters are added, or servers are already down for repair, the same 30 lets the region go dark. Work the floor out from today's load, with a margin.

A few at a time makes a wrong command slow, not right. mr-* with 3 at a time still restarts all 50 over the night, three by three, unless someone reads the count and stops it. Batches buy time to notice; they don't notice for you.

Guard rails can be switched off. A tool with a force option, or a second tool that skips the checks, puts the risk back. Keep the checks in every path that can stop servers, as AWS said it was doing when it audited its other tools.

explain.seniorTake: Every dangerous command is one typed line away from doing far more than meant, and people will always type a wrong line eventually. So make the tool the safety, not the person. Before acting, show the size of the action in numbers and ask for the number back. Offer a dry run. Refuse to go below a floor the service needs, worked out from today's load with a margin, whatever the input says. Act a few at a time, so a mistake is small and has time to be noticed. Two-person approval is good for the record and for unusual changes, but a reviewer reads the same text and shares the same blind spot. After a slip, run a blameless post-mortem that asks what let one line do this much, then fix that, and look for every other tool that could do the same: AWS audited its other operational tools after S3 in 2017.

realWorld.title: AWS S3, February 2017: one input entered incorrectly
realWorld.text: In AWS's summary of the outage of S3, its file storage service, in its Northern Virginia region (Amazon Web Services; PST is Pacific Standard Time): "At 9:37AM PST, an authorized S3 team member using an established playbook executed a command which was intended to remove a small number of servers for one of the S3 subsystems that is used by the S3 billing process. Unfortunately, one of the inputs to the command was entered incorrectly and a larger set of servers was removed than intended."

realWorld.title: AWS: the wrong servers held up two other systems
realWorld.text: "The servers that were inadvertently removed supported two other S3 subsystems." And: "Removing a significant portion of the capacity caused each of these systems to require a full restart." Like Calderline's meters, the systems needed a share of their servers up to keep working at all.

realWorld.title: AWS: a full restart took longer than expected
realWorld.text: AWS wrote that "we have not completely restarted the index subsystem or the placement subsystem in our larger regions for many years", and that "the recovery time of the index subsystem still took longer than we expected." A restart that is routine for a few servers is a different event for all of them.

realWorld.title: AWS: slower removal, and a floor
realWorld.text: "We have modified this tool to remove capacity more slowly and added safeguards to prevent capacity from being removed when it will take any subsystem below its minimum required capacity level." The fix is in the tool, not in the person: the same two rules as this case's senior answer.

realWorld.title: AWS: check the other tools too
realWorld.text: "We are also auditing our other operational tools to ensure we have similar safety checks." One guarded tool is not enough if another path can do the same thing without checks.

asked: How do you make a dangerous operation safe?
Why do two-person reviews miss things?
What is a dry run for?
interview.answer: I assume the input will be wrong one day and make the tool limit the damage. Before acting, it shows the size of the action as a number, 50 of 50 servers, and asks for that number back. It offers a dry run, which prints exactly what it would change and changes nothing, so the plan can be read, compared and kept. It refuses to go below a floor the service needs, worked out from the current load with a margin, whatever the input says. And it acts a few at a time, waiting for each batch to be healthy, so a mistake is small and slow enough to notice. Two-person reviews miss things because the reviewer reads the same text as the author: a pattern like mr-* hides its size, so both see a sensible line and neither sees 50. Reviews also become quick on routine work. I keep them for the record and for unusual changes, and put the real checks in the tool, which knows the count and the floor. AWS's S3 outage in February 2017 is the standard example: one input entered incorrectly removed more servers than intended, and AWS changed the tool to remove capacity more slowly and to refuse to go below a minimum. A story I'd tell: a power company's restart tool took a pattern meant for three meter servers and restarted all 50 at once; after 15 minutes of silence the outage map showed 180,000 homes dark while the power flowed. A minimum of 30 servers and 3 at a time would have made the same typo harmless.

terms.def: The electricity company in this story. It carries power to 180,000 homes across the Ostermere region and watches them from one control room at night.
The area Calderline Power supplies, 180,000 homes in this story.
The room where a power company's engineers watch and steer the network, day and night. Hafsa's is lit from the same lines as the homes.
A screen showing a dot for every home, lit while it has power. Calderline's shows a home dark when its smart meter has been silent for 15 minutes.
An electricity meter that sends its reading over the phone network, here every minute. A silent meter usually means a home without power.
One of the 50 servers, mr-01 to mr-50, that take the meters' readings. Each carries about 3,600 meters and can take 6,000 at most.
Stopping a program or server and starting it again. A Calderline meter server stops, checks its stored readings and starts: 20 minutes in all.
The command Calderline's engineers type in a terminal to restart meter servers, by listing names or by a pattern. As built, it restarts every match at once.
A short way to write many names at once. The tool compares it with every name and acts on all that fit. Admins also call it a glob.
Fits any characters, or none. mr-* fits every name that starts mr-, all 50 servers.
Fits exactly one character, 1, 2 or 3. mr-0[1-3] fits mr-01, mr-02 and mr-03 only.
What admins usually call a name pattern with * or [ ] in it. mr-* is a glob.
The fewest servers that must stay up to carry the work, here 30: 180,000 meters at 6,000 each. A guarded tool refuses to go below it.
Restarting servers in small groups, called batches, and waiting for each to come back before the next. A wrong pattern then stops three, not fifty.
A tool printing how many things a command will touch before it acts, '50 of 50 servers match', and asking for that number back to go on.
A check built into a tool that stops a dangerous command doing too much harm, like a railing on a mountain road: a count, a floor, a batch size or a dry run.
A second engineer who reads a command and approves it before it may run. Also called a two-person check. They see the text typed, not what it expands to.
Room kept spare above the bare minimum, so one more fault or a few more meters don't tip the service over. At exactly 30 servers, Calderline has none.
The person in the control room who sends repair crews out to faults.
Measurements from the power lines themselves, showing whether power is flowing. They told Hafsa the homes had power while the map said they did not.
The list of who is on call on which nights.
Amazon Web Services, Amazon's company that rents out computing and storage.
Amazon Simple Storage Service, AWS's service for storing files. Its February 2017 outage in Northern Virginia began with one input entered incorrectly.
One part of a larger system with its own servers. AWS named S3's index and placement subsystems, which needed a full restart in 2017.
A written set of steps for a routine job, followed by whoever is on duty. The S3 team member was using an established one.
How much work a system can carry. Removing capacity means taking servers out of service; below a minimum, the system can't keep working.
Pacific Standard Time, the winter clock time on the west coast of the United States, eight hours behind UTC.
A small group of servers acted on together. With a batch size of 3, the tool restarts three, waits for them to come back, then the next three.
Annex A controls on change management (changes to systems are controlled) and configuration management (settings are recorded and reviewed).

atWork: Look for admin tools that take a pattern, a tag or a list and act on everything they match: restart scripts, clean-up jobs, scale-down commands, delete-by-name. It is a common pattern for such a tool to print nothing before it acts and to know nothing about how much must stay up, so one wildcard that matches every server does exactly what it was told. Check four things. Does it show how many things match, before acting, and ask for that number back? Does it have a dry run? Does it refuse to go below a floor, worked out from today's load with a margin? Does it act a few at a time, waiting for each batch to be healthy? Then look for every other path that can do the same thing without those checks. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, controls A.8.32 (Change management) and A.8.9 (Configuration management) apply, and if it is pursuing SOC 2, CC8.1 expects changes to be authorized, tested and approved in a controlled way. A second approver satisfies the letter of that, but this case shows it can approve a disaster; keeping each tool's guard rails written down, and each run's printed count, who ran it and when, builds the evidence in now instead of at audit time.

recall.prompt: Your team has a clean-up tool that deletes old copies of the database by name pattern. An engineer meant to delete only last year's copies, typed a pattern that fitted every copy including last night's, and the tool deleted them in one go and printed 'done'. Your manager wants every clean-up approved by a second engineer from now on. What happened, and what would you change?

keyIdeas.idea: The tool acted on everything the pattern matched without showing how many that was
A floor: the tool refuses to go below a minimum, such as keeping the newest copies
Slow it down and preview it: a few at a time, or a dry run

recall.model: The tool did what it was told: it deleted everything the pattern fitted, in one go, and never showed how many copies that was. A second approver would read the same pattern, not the count, so it would probably pass. Change the tool. Print the count before acting and ask for it back, and offer a dry run that lists what it would delete. Make it refuse to go below a minimum: keep at least the newest seven copies, whatever the pattern says. And delete a few at a time, so a wrong pattern is noticed before it takes everything. Keep the approval for the record if you like, but don't rely on it.

recall.prompt: Why would a second engineer's approval probably not have caught restart mr-* at Calderline?
options: The approver would be less senior than Ksawery
The approver reads the same typed pattern, and nothing on the screen shows it matches 50 servers
Approvals only work in the daytime
recall.why: A pattern hides its own size. The reviewer sees restart mr-*, the same line the author saw, and it looks sensible; the 50 only appears when the tool expands it. Put the count, the floor and the batch size in the tool, which knows them.

recall.prompt: What is a dry run of a dangerous command for?
options: Running it at night, when fewer people are affected
Running it on half the servers first
Printing what it would change, such as how many servers match, without changing anything
Running it twice to check the result is the same
recall.why: A dry run shows the plan, '50 of 50 servers', and stops. It turns a pattern into a list a person can compare with what they meant. It only helps if someone reads it, so pair it with a minimum and a batch size.

recall.prompt: After its February 2017 S3 outage, what did AWS say it changed in the tool whose input was entered incorrectly?
options: Each command now needs two people to type it
It removes capacity more slowly and will not take a subsystem below its minimum required capacity
It only runs during business hours
It was retired and replaced by manual steps
recall.why: AWS wrote that it modified the tool "to remove capacity more slowly" and added safeguards against taking "any subsystem below its minimum required capacity level", and that it was auditing its other operational tools for similar checks.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. The restart tool now refuses to leave fewer than 30 servers up and restarts 3 at a time; every Tuesday since has been quiet. Over the winter a new housing estate and a heat-pump scheme added 40,000 meters: 220,000 now, on the same 50 servers, each still taking 6,000 at most. Last night 13 servers were off waiting for new disks, so 37 were up. Ksawery restarted mr-0[1-3] by the book. The tool printed '3 of 50 match. Minimum 30 up. Restarting 3 now', and 34 stayed up. At 02:15 the map showed 16,000 homes dark.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why did the minimum let this happen, and how should the tool decide how many servers it may restart?

keyIdeas.idea: The minimum of 30 was worked out for 180,000 meters and never updated; 220,000 meters need 37 servers
Work the floor out from the load each time: meters now divided by what one server carries
Keep a margin, and refuse when the servers left cannot carry every meter

coldCase.model: The guard rail worked with an old number. The 30 was right for 180,000 meters at 6,000 a server; the meters grew to 220,000 and the 30 was never updated, so it became a stale, fixed number. 220,000 divided by 6,000 is 37 servers before any spare, and the restart left 34: 204,000 meters of room, 16,000 short. Make the tool work the floor out from the load each time: count the meters now, divide by what one server carries, add a margin of a few servers, and refuse any restart that would leave fewer up than that. Servers already down for repair count against the same floor, so the tool should look at what is up, not at a fixed list.
